standard.title: Individuals and Groups in the First Nations Rights Campaign
standard.description: the contributions of significant individuals and groups in the campaign for the recognition of the rights of First Nations Australians and the extent to which they brought change to Australian society
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied significant individuals and groups in Australian history to Year 9 level, including early First Nations activists and the context of interwar rights campaigns.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students investigate the contributions of significant individuals and groups in the First Nations rights campaign and evaluate the extent to which they brought change to Australian society.

nodes.label: Significant individuals
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the contributions of significant First Nations Australians and allies in the civil rights campaign and evaluate the extent to which their work brought change.
nodes.minimum_width: Investigate the contributions of at least two significant individuals and evaluate the extent to which each brought change.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the lives and contributions of a range of significant individuals: Neville Bonner, William Cooper, Fred Maynard (AAPA), Jack Patten, Sir Douglas Nicholls, Lady Gladys Nicholls, Vincent Lingiari, Charles Perkins, Shirley Smith, Gladys Elphick, Essie Coffee, Joyce Clague, Daisy Bindi, Gary Foley, Michael Anderson, Eddie Koiki Mabo, Lowitja O'Donoghue; evaluate the extent to which each brought change — what changed, for whom, and how lasting the change was.
wider: Investigate the contributions of significant First Nations women — Gladys Elphick, Shirley Smith, Daisy Bindi, Joyce Clague, Essie Coffee — whose work has often received less historical recognition than that of male leaders, examining what their contributions reveal about how gender shaped civil rights activism

Compare the strategies of different individuals (legal action, direct action, community organising, political lobbying), evaluating which approaches were most effective in achieving specific types of change

response_modes.reason: The expanded ACARA list of individuals is deliberately diverse in gender, region, strategy, and era. Avoid teaching only the most well-known figures (Perkins, Mabo) — the breadth of the list reflects the breadth of the movement across time and place.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The breadth of significant individuals — spanning different eras, regions, strategies, and genders — offers genuine opportunities to examine how the movement evolved and how different kinds of leadership produced different kinds of change.
success_criteria: Describe the contribution of at least two significant individuals to the First Nations rights campaign
Evaluate the extent to which each identified individual brought change — specifying what changed and how lasting the change was
Identify at least one individual whose contribution is less widely known and explain why their work is historically significant

nodes.label: Significant organisations and allies
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the contributions of First Nations organisations and non-Indigenous allies (Christian, union, and labour groups) to the rights campaign, including the foundation of the National Day of Mourning.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe the contribution of at least one First Nations organisation and one non-Indigenous group to the rights campaign.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate First Nations organisations: the Australian Aborigines League (Victoria), the Australian Aboriginal Progressive Association (AAPA) and Student Action for Aborigines; examine the role of Christian, union and labour groups in the movement — including their role in the foundation of the National Day of Mourning; examine the ways some First Nations Australians' engagement with Christianity and Islam has interacted with their beliefs, identity and political freedoms.
wider: Investigate the role of Student Action for Aborigines in the 1965 Freedom Ride, examining how a student-led organisation operated alongside established First Nations organisations and what the Freedom Ride achieved

Examine the relationship between trade union support and the Wave Hill Walk-Off (1966), analysing how labour movement solidarity was both genuinely supportive and strategically complex for First Nations campaigners

response_modes.reason: This node integrates individual contributions (Node 1) with organisational and allied contributions, completing the picture of how the civil rights movement was sustained over time through collective action as well as individual leadership.

success_criteria: Describe the contribution of at least one First Nations organisation to the civil rights campaign
Explain the role of at least one non-Indigenous group (Christian, union, or student organisation) in supporting the campaign
Evaluate the extent to which organisational contributions — as distinct from individual leadership — brought change to Australian society
